1. Pre-history & Human Origins
Evolution of Homo sapiens
Paleolithic societies: hunter–gatherers, stone tools, art (Lascaux, Chauvet).
Neolithic Revolution: domestication of plants and animals, first permanent settlements (Çatalhöyük, Jericho).
Early metallurgy: copper, bronze.
Indian Subcontinent prehistoric
0) Fresh digs & rewrites (last few years)
Ancient DNA & South Asia.
• A Harappan genome from Rakhigarhi showed no Steppe pastoralist ancestry in that individual; big for timing debates on Indo-Aryan languages (2019). Cell
• Broader aDNA work (523 ancient genomes) mapped South Asian ancestry as gradients of Iranian-related + Southeast Asian–related hunter-gatherers, with Steppe-related ancestry arriving after the Indus
Sinauli “chariots” (UP). Bronze-Age burials with copper-covered carts (c. 1850–1550 BCE). Scholars dispute whether they’re true horse-drawn chariots or ox-carts. Treat as provisional. Wikipedia

Keeladi/Keeladi–Kondagai (TN). Urban features and Tamil-Brahmi material; radiocarbon points to a 6th century BCE horizon, though the earliest script dating is debated and some contexts are mixed. (New
Possible Saraswati palaeo-channel (Rajasthan, 2024–25). ASI reported a 23 m-deep palaeochannel under Bahaj village; potentially big if confirmed—but still early days. The Times of India
Gandhāran birch-bark scrolls (1st–3rd c. CE). The 1990s–present decipherment of the oldest Buddhist manuscripts continues to reshape how and where Buddhism spread (Gāndhārī/Kharoṣṭhī). Wikipedia+1
Global benchmarkers (context).
• Oldest known wooden structure, Zambia ~476,000 years (2023): pushes hominin tech back—affects deep prehistory narratives. Nature+1
• Lidar mega-surveys keep rewriting Mesoamerican urbanism (2023–25).
Indian Subcontinent History
1) Indian & subcontinental history (wide + deep, with fault lines noted)
A. Deep Prehistory → Neolithic
Earliest humans in South Asia; microlithic traditions; domestication packages (millets, rice). On rice: indica domestication involves introgression and hybrid histories—don’t oversimplify. PNAS+1
B. Indus/Harappan Civilization (c. 2600–1900 BCE core)
Urbanism (Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira), water systems, standardized weights, trade to Oman/Mesopotamia.
Script undeciphered; Dravidian/other hypotheses exist.
aDNA: Rakhigarhi individual points to no Steppe ancestry in the urban phase; later Steppe ancestry enters post-IVC. Cell+1
C. Post-Harappan & Early Vedic / Iron Age (c. 1900–600 BCE)
Regional cultures (PGW, NBPW), early iron, chiefdoms → mahājanapadas.
Sinauli material (see above) belongs around Late Harappan/Ochre-Coloured Pottery/Copper Hoard contexts; avoid over-reading. Wikipedia
D. Urban South of the Vindhyas early horizon
Keeladi/Keeladi–Kondagai complex: craft, brick structures, water works; claims of early Tamil-Brahmi use before 3rd c. BCE are contested; settle on “6th c. BCE urban horizon; earliest writing remains
E. Imperial formations & cross-roads (c. 6th–2nd c. BCE)
Achaemenid satrapies in NW; Aramaic administration intersects with Indic worlds. Kharosthi script is widely held to derive from Imperial Aramaic under the Achaemenids. Wikipedia
Mauryan Empire; Ashoka’s edicts in Prakrit, Greek, Aramaic (Kandahar bilingual & Greek edicts) demonstrate direct messaging to Hellenic audiences. edizionicafoscari.unive.it+1
F. Hellenistic, Indo-Greek, Saka, Kushan interfaces (2nd c. BCE–3rd c. CE)
Taxila/Gandhara as hubs; Greco-Buddhist art fuses Hellenistic forms with Buddhist iconography; Kushan coinage, Buddhist patronage. Encyclopedia Britannica+1
Gandhāran manuscripts (see above) anchor early Buddhist textuality in the NW. Wikipedia
G. Early Historic trade webs (1st–3rd c. CE)
Indo-Roman trade via Red Sea ports; Muziris Papyrus (Greek contract) evidences pepper/ivory shipments and legal frameworks; Berenike yields 7.5 kg pepper from India in a single jar. Oxford Academic+1
H. Classical–Early Medieval (Guptas, Deccan polities, South Indian maritime)
Sanskrit cosmopolis; math/astronomy (Āryabhaṭa, Varāhamihira, Brahmagupta); Sangam polities & Indian Ocean commerce.
Transmission outward picks up (see §3).
I. Islamic & Sultanate period; regional states (1200–1526)
Persianate court culture; regional vernaculars; technology & agrarian changes; coastal Muslim merchant networks.
J. Mughal–Early Modern (1526–1857)
High empire → regionalization; Deccan sultanates, Marathas, Sikhs; Indo-Persian knowledge ecologies; global silver flows via Indian textiles.
K. Colonial, National, Contemporary (1857–present)
Company → Crown; railways, famines, reform.
Nationalism, Partition, Republic; Green Revolution, liberalisation, tech sector, 21st-century geopolitics.
Meta-point: I’m not listing every dynasty and inscription—that’s a gazetteer. What you get here is the load-bearing scaffolding and where new evidence is moving needles.
India-centric drill-downs you can expand from here
If you want to go even deeper, pick a lane and I’ll open it up like we did with chemistry. Examples:
Epigraphy pipeline: Asokan edict corpora; Brahmi/Kharosthi palaeography; Prakrit vs Sanskrit inscriptional shifts; Greek/Aramaic edicts. edizionicafoscari.unive.it+1

Other Ancient Civilizations
Mesopotamia – Sumer, Akkad, Babylon, Assyria; writing systems (cuneiform), law codes (Hammurabi).
Ancient Egypt – Old, Middle, New Kingdoms; pyramids, pharaohs, religious beliefs.

Ancient China – Shang and Zhou dynasties; Mandate of Heaven.

Classical Mediterranean
Greece: polis, Persian wars, Athens vs Sparta, Hellenistic era.
Rome: Republic, Empire, law, Christianity’s rise.
3. Classical & Post-Classical Eras (c. 500 BCE–1500 CE)
Mauryan & Gupta empires in India.
Qin and Han China; Confucian bureaucracy.
Persian Achaemenids, Parthians, Sassanids.
Early African kingdoms: Kush, Axum.
Byzantine Empire and Eastern Orthodox world.
Rise and spread of Islam: Rashidun, Umayyad, Abbasid Caliphates.
Medieval Europe: feudalism, the Church, Crusades, scholasticism.
Mongol Empire and its Eurasian impact.
Pre-Columbian Americas: Maya, Aztec, Inca.
4. Early Modern World (c. 1500–1800)
Renaissance and Reformation in Europe.
Age of Exploration: Iberian maritime empires, Columbian exchange.
Scientific Revolution and Enlightenment.
Mughal India, Safavid Persia, Ottoman Empire.
Tokugawa Japan, Ming–Qing transition in China.
Trans-Atlantic slave trade and Atlantic economies.
Early capitalism and mercantilism.
5. The Long 19th Century (c. 1780–1914)
American and French Revolutions; Napoleonic Wars.
Industrial Revolution: technology, urbanisation, labour movements.
Nationalism: unifications of Italy and Germany.
Imperialism and the “Scramble for Africa”.
Meiji Restoration in Japan.
Social reform movements: abolition, women’s suffrage.
Scientific and intellectual shifts: Darwin, Marx, positivism.
6. The 20th Century
World War I: causes, trench warfare, Versailles Treaty.
Russian Revolution and Soviet Union.
Inter-war period: Great Depression, rise of fascism.
World War II: Axis vs Allies, Holocaust, atomic bomb.
Decolonisation: India, Africa, Southeast Asia.
Cold War: US–USSR rivalry, proxy wars, space race.
Civil rights, feminist, and liberation movements worldwide.
7. The Contemporary World (1970s–present)
End of the Cold War; collapse of the USSR.
Globalisation: trade liberalisation, internet revolution.
Rise of China and emerging economies.
Environmental history: climate change, sustainability debates.
Terrorism and 9/11, Middle Eastern conflicts.
Digital era: social media, information economy.
8. Cross-Cutting Themes
Economic history: agrarian economies, industrial capitalism, global trade systems.
Intellectual history: philosophies, religions, science and technology.
Social history: gender roles, family structures, class relations.
Environmental & climate history.
History of medicine and public health.
Historiography: schools of thought (Marxist, Annales, post-colonial, microhistory).
